candidato.titulo: Brain PET scans help select and monitor patients for new Alzheimer's drugs
candidato.resumo: Nuclear medicine is playing an increasingly important role in the diagnosis and treatment of Alzheimer's disease, helping clinicians visualize the biological changes associated with the condition and guide decisions about new therapies. Amyloid PET imaging is being used to confirm the presence of amyloid pathology and support treatment decisions for patients receiving anti-amyloid drugs, while tau PET scans can provide additional information about disease progression and prognosis.

texto_fonte:
Brain PET scans help select and monitor patients for new Alzheimer's drugs
Nuclear medicine is playing an increasingly important role in the diagnosis and treatment of Alzheimer's disease, helping clinicians visualize the biological changes associated with the condition and guide decisions about new therapies. Amyloid PET imaging is being used to confirm the presence of amyloid pathology and support treatment decisions for patients receiving anti-amyloid drugs, while tau PET scans can provide additional information about disease progression and prognosis.
At the 39th Annual Congress of the European Association of Nuclear Medicine (EANM'26), taking place from Oct. 17 to 21 in Vienna, experts will discuss first experiences with these PET scans in routine clinical use and explore the latest advances in nuclear medicine.
"Molecular imaging enables us to visualize functions and target structures using targeted tracers. This is vital for delivering precision medicine and tailoring treatment to the individual patient," says Matthias Brendel, deputy director of the Department of Nuclear Medicine at LMU Munich. "Enormous progress is being made, particularly in the characterization and therapeutic monitoring of neurodegenerative diseases, above all in Alzheimer's disease."
Confirming the diagnosis before treatment
According to the World Health Organization, 57 million people were living with dementia worldwide in 2021. Alzheimer's disease is the most common form of dementia, accounting for 60% to 70% of all cases.
"With an amyloid PET scan we can visualize the amyloid in the brain of a person with dementia and determine whether it is actually Alzheimer's disease or another form of dementia," explains Brendel. "This is important because the new therapy using monoclonal antibodies against beta-amyloid—lecanemab and donanemab, which have been approved in recent years by the FDA and the European Commission—can only be effective in cases of Alzheimer's disease."
Blood and cerebrospinal fluid biomarkers can also support the diagnosis but in many cases leave some uncertainty, according to Brendel, who recommends an amyloid PET scan for confirmation before starting treatment.
Showing how treatment is working
Amyloid PET can also help clinicians monitor the response to treatment. "The scan shows at what point the amyloid level in the brain falls below the detection limit, meaning the scan is amyloid-negative. Many patients experience this after taking donanemab for 12 months, even though the treatment is generally designed to last 1.5 years.
"In a phase 3 trial for donanemab published in the Journal of the American Medical Association (JAMA), 52% of participants who received the drug completed their entire course of treatment in less than 12 months. Once the amyloid has been cleared, clinicians may be able to consider ending treatment," says the nuclear medicine specialist.
Treating Alzheimer's before symptoms progress
Amyloid-beta is a protein that occurs naturally in the brain. In people with Alzheimer's disease, it accumulates between the brain cells, initially forming small clumps and later developing into large plaques. This process begins years before the first symptoms.
"The tracers used in PET scans bind to the compact plaques and visualize them, while the drugs act on the early aggregates and can therefore slow the progression of the disease by up to 30% at an early stage, according to clinical trials," points out Brendel.
The earlier treatment can be started, the better, according to the nuclear medicine specialist. Lecanemab and donanemab are therefore aimed at patients in the early stages of the disease, with mild cognitive impairment or mild dementia.
Tau PET: predicting the course of the disease
In Alzheimer's disease, amyloid-beta works together with another protein, tau, to disrupt communication between nerve cells, which then die off progressively. Although no approved drug yet targets tau deposits, tau PET scans are already of great value, says Brendel.
"At our clinic alone, more than 500 amyloid and tau PET scans are carried out each year to diagnose Alzheimer's disease. Using the tracer employed at the LMU Medical Centre, we also obtain a binding curve which allows us to determine whether there are amyloid-beta-associated tau deposits and to assess the extent of neuronal damage. This enables us to make accurate predictions regarding the progression of the disease and the likelihood of a positive response to treatment."
Clinical trials with donanemab showed that patients with low levels of tau respond better to the new drugs than those with high levels of tau in the brain, according to Brendel. "Amyloid PET is important for establishing a definitive diagnosis of Alzheimer's in general," says the nuclear medicine specialist. "Tau PET has the greatest potential because it can help us determine, with a high degree of certainty, who is particularly suitable for the therapies that are already available and who would benefit little from them."
Looking ahead: a new antibody in development
A phase 3 trial for trontinemab, an amyloid antibody that crosses the blood-brain barrier using its own shuttle mechanism, is currently underway. "This could significantly increase the availability of the antibody in the brain and reduce side effects. Treatment could then be completed more quickly, possibly within three to four months. Here too, amyloid PET would be needed to confirm that treatment has been successful, but we must, of course, await the completion of the regulatory approval trials," adds Brendel.

candidato.titulo: Optical imaging links altered metabolism and oxygen use in Alzheimer's disease
candidato.resumo: Alzheimer's disease is best known for its effects on memory and cognition, but the disease also involves changes in how brain cells produce and use energy. Mitochondria, the structures that supply much of a cell's energy, can become dysfunctional in Alzheimer's disease. At the same time, changes in blood flow and oxygen availability may place additional demands on brain tissue. Understanding how these processes interact could help researchers characterize metabolic changes that accompany the disease.

texto_fonte:
Optical imaging links altered metabolism and oxygen use in Alzheimer's disease
Alzheimer's disease is best known for its effects on memory and cognition, but the disease also involves changes in how brain cells produce and use energy. Mitochondria, the structures that supply much of a cell's energy, can become dysfunctional in Alzheimer's disease. At the same time, changes in blood flow and oxygen availability may place additional demands on brain tissue. Understanding how these processes interact could help researchers characterize metabolic changes that accompany the disease.
A recent study published in Neurophotonics examines these processes together in the living brain. Researchers in Ammasi Periasamy's group at the University of Virginia (UVA) combined two forms of two-photon lifetime microscopy to measure cellular metabolism and oxygen levels in the cerebral cortex of mice. They compared Alzheimer's disease model mice with healthy, wild-type mice.
The approach addresses an important difficulty in studying brain metabolism. Oxygen supply and cellular energy production are closely related, but measurements of one do not necessarily reveal what is happening to the other. By collecting both types of information at the same time, the researchers could examine how metabolic activity relates to oxygen availability within the same living tissue.
Measuring metabolism through autofluorescence
To track cellular metabolism, the team used two-photon fluorescence lifetime imaging microscopy, or FLIM. Rather than simply measuring the brightness of fluorescence, FLIM measures how long fluorescent molecules remain in an excited state before releasing light.
The researchers focused on NAD(P)H, a naturally occurring molecule involved in cellular energy production. NAD(P)H can exist either freely within cells or bound to proteins, and these states have different fluorescence lifetimes. The study used the proportion of protein-bound NAD(P)H as an indicator of mitochondrial metabolic activity. Because NAD(P)H occurs naturally in cells, its fluorescence provides a way to examine metabolism without introducing a fluorescent label specifically for that measurement.
The second technique, phosphorescence lifetime imaging microscopy, or PLIM, provided information about oxygen. Here the researchers used an oxygen-sensitive ruthenium-based probe. Its phosphorescence lifetime changes in response to oxygen concentration, allowing the investigators to estimate the partial pressure of oxygen, or pO₂, in the brain's vascular network. Combining FLIM and PLIM therefore provided simultaneous measurements related to cellular metabolism and vascular oxygenation.
Metabolism and oxygen differ in the Alzheimer's model
"FLIM and PLIM simultaneous measurement requires precise synchronization between the Zeiss two-photon microscope and the Becker & Hickl lifetime-imaging electronics," says Periasamy, professor and director of the W.M. Keck Center for Cellular Imaging at UVA. "This lets us capture metabolism and oxygen tension at the same moment, in live animals. Careful calibration, together with stable physiological conditions such as body temperature and anesthesia, turns these lifetime signals into reliable oxygen measurements. It allows us to see how oxygen supply in arteries, capillaries and veins relates to metabolic changes in the living brain."
The measurements revealed clear differences between the two groups while the anesthetized animals were at rest. The cortices of the Alzheimer's disease model mice showed a higher protein-bound fraction of NAD(P)H than those of wild-type animals, indicating altered mitochondrial metabolic activity.
At the same time, oxygen measurements told a related story. Oxygen partial pressure in the cortical vascular network was lower in the Alzheimer's model than in the wild-type mice. The researchers interpret this lower vascular oxygen level as evidence of greater oxygen consumption in the Alzheimer's disease model.
Andrés Norambuena, senior scientist at UVA and co-author of the study, remarks, "Taken together, the findings suggest that changes in cellular energy metabolism and oxygen use can be detected concurrently in the living Alzheimer's disease mouse brain. That connection matters because mitochondrial dysfunction and impaired cerebral oxygenation have both been implicated in Alzheimer's disease, yet they are often investigated separately."
The work also demonstrates the value of viewing brain physiology through several measurements at once. Two-photon FLIM-PLIM can provide metabolic and oxygen information in living tissue with relatively little disruption, allowing researchers to examine relationships that are harder to resolve from isolated measurements.
The results come from a mouse model, so they do not establish that the same metabolic and oxygen patterns occur in people with Alzheimer's disease. Instead, the study provides an imaging framework for investigating how oxygen availability and mitochondrial metabolism change together as neurological disease develops. By measuring both processes in vivo, researchers may gain a more complete view of the physiological changes that accompany Alzheimer's disease.
More information
Vijay Kumar Sagar et al., Metabolism and oxygen tension in Alzheimer's disease mouse model using two-photon FLIM-PLIM microscopy, Neurophotonics (2026). DOI: 10.1117/1.nph.13.3.035008

candidato.titulo: The rise of the machines is canceled: Why humanoids with AI are helpers, not enemies
candidato.resumo: Humans play a key role in developing humanoid robots and training AI models, so we can maintain control, writes a columnist. The post The rise of the machines is canceled: Why humanoids with AI are helpers, not enemies appeared first on The Robot Report .

texto_fonte:
For decades, engineers have been trying to create robots that look and act like humans. Now, rapid advances in artificial intelligence are bringing humanoid robots out of the lab and onto the factory floor. As fears grow that AI will displace workers, a global race is underway to develop humanoid robots capable of performing human work.
Competitors include Tesla, startups backed by Amazon and NVIDIA, and state-owned Chinese companies. Waltham, Mass.-based Boston Dynamics, valued at over $1 billion, is among the humanoid leaders with its Atlas robot. South Korean automaker Hyundai owns an 88% stake in the company.
Hyundai‘s massive auto plant is arguably the most advanced in the world. More than 1,000 robots work alongside nearly 1,500 humans, lifting, stamping, and welding parts in robotic unison. Atlas, at 175 cm (68.8 in.) tall and 90 kg (198.4 lb.) in weight, has left the lab and is doing real work.
Atlas and AI learn with human help
Atlas’s development is led by Zach Jackowski. He holds two degrees in mechanical engineering from MIT, and his mission is to transform the robot into a productive worker on the factory floor. Atlas confidently helps sort roof racks for the assembly line without human intervention. It operates autonomously; many roboticists would have considered this insane five or six years ago.
In 2021, Atlas was a bulky, hydraulic robot that could only run and jump. Back then, Atlas relied on algorithms written by engineers. The next-generation Atlas, with its sleek, all-electric body and AI, runs on cutting-edge NVIDIA chips, making it intelligent enough to autonomously perform incredible stunts.
Scott Kindersma led robotics research department at Boston Dynamics before moving to Google DeepMind. He explained that modern robots have learned to master movements that until recently were considered too complex for a machine. This is largely due to how these robots are programmed: more emphasis is placed on demonstrations and machine learning than on manual programming.
This humanoid can learn. Atlas learns in a variety of ways. In supervised training, machine learning specialist Kevin Bergerman (now also at Google DeepMind), wearing a virtual reality headset, took direct control of the humanoid, guiding its hand and arm movements step by step through each task until Atlas masters it. If this teleoperator can perform the task we want the robot to perform, this generates data that is subsequently used to train the robot’s AI models to perform that task autonomously.
The stylish suit you wear will actually record all your body movements to train Atlas to accurately mimic your movements. In this way, you will serve as a physical prototype for a 200-lb. metal robot. All your movements—walking, hand gestures—are captured by these sensors.
Engineers then feed this data into a machine learning process. Atlas’s body is different from yours, so they had to teach it to virtually imitate human movements. Over 4,000 digital Atlases were trained for six hours in a simulation. The simulation added complex challenges for the avatars, such as slippery floors, bending, and stiff joints.
Ultimately, this could lead to many copies of Atlas, each having loaded new skills into the AI system. Once one robot is trained, they are all trained. Using the same processes, Atlas was taught to crawl and cartwheel. It wasn’t as good at duck walking.
Indeed, Atlas, or any other humanoid, can’t yet do most of the things a person does in their daily lives. For example, simply getting dressed in the morning or pouring a cup of coffee and carrying it around the house are too complex for Atlas.
What particularly stands out about Atlas is its brain. NVIDIA chips—the same ones that helped launch the AI revolution with GPT chat—process a stream of collected data, bringing this humanoid robot closer to a semblance of common sense. Atlas can see its surroundings and understands how the physical world works.
One day, you’ll be able to place such a robot in a factory and simply explain to it what you want it to do. It will have enough knowledge of how the world works to perform the tasks assigned to it.
Spot platform demonstrates legged robot utility
There’s currently a lot of excitement in the industry about the potential of creating robots smart enough to be truly versatile. Robert Playter, CEO of Boston Dynamics, led the company’s robotics development until stepping down earlier this year.
The cornerstone was the robotic dog Spot, introduced almost 10 years ago. The quadruped is trained to work in hot, cold, and rugged conditions, roaming the halls of Boston Dynamics.
It has multiple cameras, thermal sensors, acoustic sensors, and an array of sensors on its back that allow it to collect data on the plant’s condition. Spot conducts quality checks at the Hyundai plant, ensuring that cars are equipped with the necessary parts. They conduct safety checks and industrial inspections at hundreds of facilities around the world. What began with Spot has evolved into Atlas. This robot is capable of superhuman movement.
Therefore, it will be able to surpass what we can do. “So, you’re creating a robot that should surpass human capabilities.”
“Why not, right? We’d love to invent creatures that could be stronger than us, withstand higher temperatures than us, or enter dangerous places.” Superhuman capabilities—for many people, that sounds terrifying. You’re not envisioning a Terminator world.
Absolutely not. If you saw how hard it takes to get robots to perform some of the simple tasks required of them, it would allay fears about intelligent and out-of-control machines. Could people have more pressing concerns?
It’s guaranteed that there will be people who say, “I’ll lose my job to a robot.” Work is truly changing. So monotonous, grueling work will eventually be performed by robots.
But these robots aren’t so autonomous that they don’t need to be managed. They need to be built, trained, and maintained. It could be several years before Atlas joins the Hyundai team permanently. Goldman Sachs predicts the humanoid robot market will reach $38 billion within a decade.
The humanoid robot race continues
Boston Dynamics and other U.S. robot makers are vying for the lead, but they’re not alone in the competition. Chinese companies are proving themselves to be formidable competitors. They’re determined to win.
Are they ahead of us?
The Chinese government is on a mission: to win the robotics race. Technically, we’re still ahead, but there’s a real risk that, simply due to the scale of our investments, we could fall behind.
To stay ahead, Hyundai has made a major investment in Boston Dynamics. This is the beginning of a long journey. The ultimate goal is the human-like future we mentioned at the beginning. Robots like us, working alongside us, walking among us.
Editor’s note: Physical AI and humanoids are among the session track topics at RoboBusiness 2026, which will be on Oct. 20 and 21 in Santa Clara, Calif. Register now to attend.
AI moves toward superhuman capabilities
When Demis Hassabis won the Nobel Prize in 2024, he celebrated by playing poker with the world chess champion. Hassabis loves games, which is how he became an artificial intelligence pioneer. The British scientist is co-founder and CEO of Google DeepMind.
A few years ago, chatbots heralded a new era. Now, Hassabis and others are striving to create what’s known as artificial general intelligence—a silicon-based intelligence as versatile as a human, but with superhuman speed and knowledge.
“I’ve always been driven and intrigued by understanding the world around us,” said Hassabis. “Since childhood, I’ve been fascinated by big questions: the meaning of life, the nature of consciousness, the nature of reality itself.”
“I loved reading about the great scientists and philosophers who worked on these problems, and I wanted to see if we could advance human knowledge,” he recalled. “For me, the expression of this desire has been the creation of what I consider the perfect tool for advancing human knowledge: artificial intelligence.”
Hassabis noted that AI is advancing quickly, attracting attention, resources, and talent. Early chatbots only explored the internet. An app called Astra perceives the world. It was able to make up stories after being shown paintings. But such systems are still learning about context and may develop unexpected skills.
“So, new capabilities or properties may emerge as a result of learning. This may worry people,” Hassabis acknowledged. “The duality of these types of systems is that they are capable of incredible things, going beyond what we can design or understand ourselves.”
From AGI to robotics
As AI begins to take on tasks such as booking flights and shopping online, it is taking steps toward AGI. By 2030, we could have systems that truly understand their surroundings and are integrated into our daily lives. This is where robots come in.
Once a robot can perceive, understand, decide, and act, it can begin to do truly useful things. Researchers Alex Lee and Julia Vassallo have demonstrated a robot that understands what it sees. It’s not easy. And it reasons by following vague instructions. “Place the blocks whose colors correspond to the combination of yellow and blue into the corresponding ball.” The combination of yellow and blue is green. And the robot figured it out.
Is Hassabis working on a system that would be self-aware?
“I don’t think any modern system feels self-aware or, you know, conscious in any sense,” he replied. “Obviously, everyone needs to make their own decisions when interacting with these chatbots. I think it’s theoretically possible. But is self-awareness your goal? It might happen implicitly. These systems might acquire some sense of self-awareness. It’s important for these systems to understand you, themselves, and others, and that’s the beginning of self-awareness.”
“If a machine becomes self-aware, we might not recognize it,” continued Hassabis. “There are two reasons why we consider each other conscious. One is that you exhibit the behavior of a conscious being. The second is that you operate on the same foundation. We are made of the same carbon material, and our brains are soft and flexible. Machines operate on silicon. So, even if they exhibit the same behavior and say the same things, that doesn’t necessarily mean the sense of consciousness we experience is the same as theirs.”
Hassabis told us that AI could lead to what he called “radical abundance,” the elimination of scarcity. But he also gave a warning.
“There are two things that worry me. One is that malicious actors will repurpose these systems for harm,” said Hassabis. “The second question concerns the AI systems themselves. As they become increasingly autonomous and powerful, can we ensure that we can control these systems, that they align with our values, that they do what we want, that they benefit society, and that they remain within established constraints?”
Can an AI agent be taught morality? “I think so,” Hassabis responded. “They learn by doing, by teaching others. And I think this is one of the challenges we must address: giving them a value system, guidance, and some constraints, just like we teach a child.”
Google DeepMind is competing with dozens of other companies striving to create AGI that you won’t be able to distinguish from human intelligence. It announced its Gemini 2 foundation model in August and Gemini 4 Argon this week.
Anduril founder says robots and AI can reduce risk
Some international groups call such weapons killer robots. But Palmer Luckey, founder of Anduril Industries, said they represent the future of warfare—a working product that eliminates risks. Once a child prodigy, Luckey sold Oculus to Facebook for $2 billion.
He ultimately decided to move into the defense industry. The billionaire owns an autonomous speedboat called Dive XL. It is not remote-controlled, and Anduril claimed that it can travel 1,000 miles fully submerged. Australia has already invested $58 million in such submarines.
Tucked away inside a hangar is an Anduril unmanned fighter jet called the Fury. It has no cockpit, control stick, or rudder because there’s no pilot. Some in the defense industry viewed Anduril as just another tech startup until it beat out several leading defense contractors in the competition to build an unmanned fighter jet for the U.S. Air Force.
About the author
Elena Krosheva is a freelance journalist, marketing analyst, and SEO specialist. She graduated with honors from the Faculty of Journalism at the Institute of Modern Knowledge in Minsk, Belarus, in 2007.
Krosheva covers topics such as digitalization, IT, the modern economy, and transhumanism. She loves computers and cyberpunk, having graduated from a technical college before graduating from the Faculty of Journalism.

candidato.titulo: Microsoft se rende e lança antivírus do Windows para Linux
candidato.resumo: A Microsoft anunciou a chegada do seu antivírus Defender aos computadores com Linux. A novidade, divulgada na quarta-feira (14), permite que empresas utilizem a ferramenta de segurança da criadora do Windows em desktops com sistemas como Ubuntu, Debian e Fedora. O recurso já está disponível em versão de testes. Segundo a empresa, a expansão do Microsoft Defender for Endpoint tem como principal público os desenvolvedores e profissionais de tecnologia que utilizam Linux no trabalho. A ferramenta permite identificar ameaças, monitorar atividades suspeitas e proteger computadores que possuem acesso a informações corporativas. Apesar da novidade, o Defender já funcionava em servidores Linux desde 2020. A mudança anunciada agora amplia oficialmente o suporte para computadores de trabalho, permitindo que empresas adotem a mesma solução de segurança em diferentes sistemas operacionais. O que o antivírus da Microsoft faz no Linux? A nova versão do Defender oferece ferramentas semelhantes às utilizadas pela Microsoft para proteger computadores com Windows e servidores Linux. Entre os recursos estão a identificação de vírus e outros programas maliciosos, a detecção de comportamentos suspeitos

texto_fonte:
Microsoft se rende e lança antivírus do Windows para Linux
Por Marcelo Fischer |
A Microsoft anunciou a chegada do seu antivírus Defender aos computadores com Linux. A novidade, divulgada na quarta-feira (14), permite que empresas utilizem a ferramenta de segurança da criadora do Windows em desktops com sistemas como Ubuntu, Debian e Fedora. O recurso já está disponível em versão de testes.
Segundo a empresa, a expansão do Microsoft Defender for Endpoint tem como principal público os desenvolvedores e profissionais de tecnologia que utilizam Linux no trabalho.
A ferramenta permite identificar ameaças, monitorar atividades suspeitas e proteger computadores que possuem acesso a informações corporativas.
Apesar da novidade, o Defender já funcionava em servidores Linux desde 2020. A mudança anunciada agora amplia oficialmente o suporte para computadores de trabalho, permitindo que empresas adotem a mesma solução de segurança em diferentes sistemas operacionais.
O que o antivírus da Microsoft faz no Linux?
A nova versão do Defender oferece ferramentas semelhantes às utilizadas pela Microsoft para proteger computadores com Windows e servidores Linux.
Entre os recursos estão a identificação de vírus e outros programas maliciosos, a detecção de comportamentos suspeitos e o monitoramento de vulnerabilidades que podem ser exploradas por criminosos.
O software também possui um sistema chamado EDR (detecção e resposta em endpoints), que permite identificar possíveis ataques e investigar atividades realizadas nos dispositivos.
Caso uma ameaça seja detectada, os administradores podem executar comandos remotamente e até isolar o computador da rede para impedir que um ataque se espalhe.
A Microsoft justifica o lançamento pelo uso crescente de Linux entre desenvolvedores. Segundo a empresa, esses computadores frequentemente possuem acesso a repositórios de códigos, serviços em nuvem e ferramentas internas que podem ser exploradas em ataques cibernéticos.
Com a novidade, equipes de segurança poderão acompanhar computadores Linux, Windows e macOS em uma plataforma centralizada.
Quem pode usar o Microsoft Defender no Linux?
Por enquanto, a novidade está disponível em prévia pública e exige uma assinatura corporativa. O antivírus gratuito que acompanha o Windows não está sendo oferecido aos usuários domésticos de Linux.
Segundo a documentação da Microsoft, o suporte aos desktops está incluído nas seguintes licenças: Microsoft Defender for Endpoint Plano 2 (P2), Microsoft 365 E5 e Microsoft 365 E7.
O software pode ser instalado nas distribuições Linux que já eram compatíveis com a ferramenta de segurança para servidores. A relação inclui Ubuntu, Debian, Fedora, Red Hat Enterprise Linux, CentOS, openSUSE e outras versões do sistema.
Além disso, a Microsoft informa que os mesmos métodos de instalação utilizados nos servidores poderão ser aproveitados pelos administradores para configurar o Defender nos computadores de trabalho.
A empresa ainda não informou quando a nova modalidade deixará a fase de testes e será lançada em sua versão definitiva.
Microsoft já considerou o Linux uma ameaça
A chegada do Defender aos desktops Linux representa mais um capítulo de uma relação que mudou bastante nas últimas décadas.
Em 2001, o então CEO da Microsoft, Steve Ballmer, chegou a comparar o Linux a um "câncer", ao criticar o modelo de licenciamento de softwares de código aberto. Na época, a empresa enxergava o sistema como um concorrente do Windows.
Essa postura mudou com a chegada de Satya Nadella ao comando da Microsoft. Em 2014, o executivo apresentou publicamente a mensagem "Microsoft ama Linux", reforçando uma estratégia de aproximação com o sistema operacional.
Desde então, a companhia ampliou seu suporte ao Linux em produtos de nuvem, ferramentas para desenvolvedores e soluções de segurança. A chegada do Defender aos desktops é mais uma etapa dessa expansão.

candidato.titulo: Taiwan targets illicit AI server exports to China with five-year prison terms
candidato.resumo: Taiwan is expanding the Foreign Trade Act to include AI servers and semiconductors in its list of controlled exports.

texto_fonte:
Taiwan is expanding its list of controlled exports to include AI servers and the latest chips in a move to align its policies with the U.S.’s trade bans. Bloomberg reports that after the export controls take effect, anyone caught smuggling these items will be criminally charged under the Foreign Trade Act, which carries a penalty of up to five years in prison and/or a fine of around $92,500.
“Going forward, some of our measures on controlled items will correspond to American ones because we have made quite some commitments in the Agreement on Reciprocal Trade,” Taiwan Minister of Economic Affairs Kung Ming-hsin said. The two parties signed the trade deal earlier this year, which saw the U.S. cutting tariffs on Taiwanese goods down to 15% in exchange for direct investments in the U.S. tech industry, among others.
The U.S. has long been trying to stamp out the smuggling of advanced Nvidia chips into China. One of the biggest cases that U.S. authorities have prosecuted so far includes three Super Micro employees, including its co-founder Yih-Shyan “Wally” Liaw, who are accused of smuggling $2.5 billion worth of AI servers. A few months after this revelation, Taiwanese authorities raided Super Micro’s Taipei offices in connection with the Nvidia B300 smuggling probe, which eventually led to the indictment of nine individuals related to the case.
Since Taiwan doesn’t treat AI chip exports to China as a crime before this new set of export controls is enacted, people violating the chip bans would have to be charged under other laws. This is what Singapore did when it arrested suspected Nvidia AI GPU smugglers — because it doesn’t have a law that prohibits the export of advanced AI chips to China, it instead charged the individuals with fraud and money laundering.
The expansion of the Foreign Trade Act will be one of the strictest measures that the Taiwanese government has put into place against exports to China, which is something that it has been considering earlier this year. This move will likely please Washington as it pressures other countries to take more steps in its controlling the flow of advanced AI chips into China. However, it will also likely provoke Beijing, which has already condemned Taipei after it applied export restrictions on Huawei and SMIC last year.

texto_fonte:
This NASA Hubble Space Telescope image features the edge-on, intermediate spiral galaxy NGC 1827, located roughly 37 million light-years away in the constellation Columba, the Dove. Hubble captured the image as part of a survey looking at 260 satellite galaxies around 22 Milky Way-like host galaxies within a radius of about 32 million light-years from Earth. Hubble has already observed 111 of these satellite galaxies. The remaining galaxies will take an additional 149 Hubble orbits, one orbit for each galaxy, to observe.
The image, taken with Hubble’s Advanced Camera for Surveys, reveals bright-blue regions along the galaxy’s disk dotted with dark dust lanes where new stars are likely forming. A bright foreground star appears just to the left of the galaxy’s bright central bulge but is located between us and the galaxy. Its four diffraction spikes are the result of light bending around the internal supports that hold Hubble’s secondary mirror.
Low-mass galaxies like the ones in this Hubble observing program provide a way to test the predictions of cosmological models on small scales, which struggle to match observations. The data Hubble gathers will help us better understand and characterize the properties of low-mass galaxies in Milky Way-like systems, allowing researchers to refine cosmological models.

candidato.titulo: Anthropic’s Claude Designs Leaner Quantum Circuits, Reducing Resources Needed for Key Calculations
candidato.resumo: Insider Brief A team of researchers from Anthropic and Harvard used an artificial intelligence (AI) system to design quantum circuits that require fewer operations and qubits, potentially lowering the hardware demands of useful quantum computing. The researchers, who posted their work on the preprint server arXiv, tested the approach on eight computational building blocks used […]

texto_fonte:
Insider Brief
- Anthropic and Harvard researchers used Claude to design more efficient quantum circuits across eight tasks, reducing estimated computing resources for key routines used in quantum algorithms.
- One redesigned decoding circuit used roughly 12 times fewer costly quantum operations, while a new arithmetic design offered improved trade-offs between gate counts and qubit requirements.
- The results were evaluated through computational checks and resource estimates rather than demonstrations on quantum hardware, and practical benefits will depend on integration into complete algorithms and machines.
A team of researchers from Anthropic and Harvard used an artificial intelligence (AI) system to design quantum circuits that require fewer operations and qubits, potentially lowering the hardware demands of useful quantum computing.
The researchers, who posted their work on the preprint server arXiv, tested the approach on eight computational building blocks used in chemistry, optimization, physics simulation and number theory. Seven of those designs reduced both the number of costly quantum operations and the number of qubits compared with the study’s baselines. The eighth produced a new approach to arithmetic that offers better choices between computing time and memory.
The results concern circuit designs and resource estimates, rather than calculations demonstrated on a working quantum computer. The team nevertheless addressed a central problem for the industry that, in order for quantum computers to become more useful quantum, algorithms will need to improve computing alongside the development larger, more reliable machines.
According to the study, one redesigned decoding circuit required about 440,000 Toffoli gates, down from 5.1 million in the comparison design, while reducing its peak qubit requirement from 1,938 to 1,837. Toffoli gates are operations that are particularly costly in many proposed error-corrected quantum computers, making their number a useful measure of computational work.
The research also illustrates a potential role for AI in scientific development, according to an accompanying blog post on the work. Rather than asking a model simply to suggest ideas, the team gave it programming tools and an evaluator that checked proposed circuits and scored their resource requirements. The model could then revise its designs in response to concrete feedback.
Anthropic’s blog post identifies the model as Claude Mythos 5 and says its elliptic-curve arithmetic work took 53 hours, with human involvement limited to the initial instructions and occasional prompts to broaden its search.
Reducing the Cost of Quantum Computation
A quantum circuit is a sequence of operations applied to qubits, the units that store quantum information. Larger algorithms depend on smaller routines that perform arithmetic, retrieve data or calculate numerical functions.
Making those routines cheaper can reduce the requirements of the larger computation. But translating an efficient conventional algorithm into a quantum circuit introduces constraints that can consume much of the original advantage.
For the circuits examined in the study, calculations must preserve the information needed to reverse their operations. Temporary results cannot simply be overwritten as they would be in ordinary software. Instead, the circuit must clear its scratch work through a process called — ironically enough — uncomputation.
Keeping temporary results uses additional qubits and clearing them early can require repeating calculations later, increasing the number of gates, which are the computing steps for a quantum computer. Circuit designers must balance those competing costs.
The researchers’ AI search repeatedly found ways to recover information from the current state of a calculation rather than store a separate record of every earlier decision. Other improvements allowed different computational paths to share the same arithmetic operations.
A third strategy reduced resources reserved for rare, unusually demanding inputs. Where a task allowed a small probability of failure, the model could omit machinery needed only for those exceptional cases, the researchers write in the study.
These changes went beyond removing redundant gates from an existing design. They involved choosing algorithms, organizing data and planning how intermediate calculations would be reversed.
A Smaller Decoder and a New Arithmetic Design
One major result involved decoded quantum interferometry, or DQI, an algorithm that uses the wave-like behavior of quantum states to reinforce better answers and suppress poorer ones, making better solutions more likely when the result is measured.
The researchers examined a decoding routine used within DQI for a mathematical curve-fitting problem. This decoder identifies errors from a compact set of checks. Although it borrows techniques from error-correcting codes, its role here is inside the optimization algorithm, rather than correcting faults in the quantum hardware.
The AI-designed circuit replaced an approach based on the extended Euclidean algorithm with a method called Berlekamp–Massey. The replacement offered more efficient arithmetic, but a straightforward reversible implementation would have required substantial memory for intermediate information.
The new circuit avoided much of that storage by reconstructing information when needed.
According to the paper, one remaining storage requirement could reach 665 qubits in the worst case. The discovered design allocated 19 qubits instead, accepting failure on rare inputs that exceeded that capacity. A second stored entry was needed with a probability of about one in 10,000 under the specified input distribution.
Together, the changes reduced the decoder’s gate count by roughly a factor of 12.
Another result discussed by the researchers was focused on modular inversion, a type of division using numbers that cycle like the hours on a clock. It is a central operation in elliptic-curve calculations used in quantum algorithms relevant to cryptography.
The model developed a reversible implementation of divsteps, a conventional arithmetic method whose memory requirements had made it difficult to use efficiently in this quantum setting.
The key was recovering earlier computational decisions from patterns in the numbers that remained available. The study presents a mathematical proof explaining why that information could be recovered.
Recovering every decision was not always the cheapest option, however. The resulting circuit family combines reconstruction and storage in different proportions, allowing designers to choose between fewer qubits and fewer gates.
The study reports one complete benchmark circuit using about 4 million Toffoli gates and 935 qubits. Those figures describe an arithmetic component, not the resources required for an entire cryptographic attack.
Other tasks that showed savings included a circuit for calculating a fixed-point Gaussian function that reduced the product of gate count and qubit count by a factor of 39. A numerical routine associated with solving linear equations also improved that combined measure by a factor of 32, according to the paper.
What the Results Establish
The researchers began each search with a written task specification and a blank program. The model proposed several different algorithmic approaches, which were developed in parallel, with promising ideas shared between them.
An independent evaluator tested proposed circuits and ranked them by the number of Toffoli gates multiplied by peak qubit use.
This worked because the team selected a class of circuits whose behavior can be checked efficiently on conventional computers. General quantum circuits can be much harder to simulate, limiting how broadly the same process can be applied.
The comparisons also require care. For one of the seven tasks with lower gate and qubit counts, involving a Hermitian-code decoder, the researchers report that no previous reversible implementation existed in the literature. Its baseline was a straightforward reversible construction, rather than an established published quantum circuit.
The supplementary material describes extensive sampled tests and, for some components, exhaustive checks. Sampling can provide evidence of correctness and estimate rare failures, but it does not prove that every possible input will succeed.
The scoring system is also an approximation because actual execution costs depend on gate and qubit counts, hardware connections, operation scheduling, measurements and the system used to correct errors. A circuit with a better score under the study’s metric may not be the best choice for every machine.
Claude also showed limitations as a research tool. In early experiments, it favored established approaches and repeatedly checked apparent improvements, sometimes continuing after the results were already well supported, according to Anthropic’s post. That caution helped verify its work but could also discourage exploration of unfamiliar methods.
The researchers addressed this by requiring Claude to develop several distinct approaches in parallel and occasionally prompting it to broaden its search. According to the post, those interventions encouraged more ambitious designs, including the new approach to reversible modular inversion. Once Claude identified that approach, it developed, implemented and verified it autonomously.
From Individual Circuits to Larger Systems
The researchers propose extending the approach to coordinate decisions that are usually made separately, including algorithms, error-correcting codes and the physical architecture of a quantum computer.
That would require evaluators capable of tracking how changes in one part affect resource demands elsewhere. The study identifies designing an appropriate scoring system as a matter that still requires application and hardware judgment.
The immediate result is narrower but useful. AI-guided searches produced circuit designs that reduce the estimated cost of several important computational routines and, in modular inversion, developed a new reversible arithmetic structure.
The research team included Andi Gu, of Anthropic’s STEM Fellows Program and Harvard; Alek H. Kemeny, of Anthropic and Susanne F. Yelin and Mikhail D. Lukin, both of Harvard University. Lukin is also co-founder and Chief Scientist of QuEra Computing.
For a deeper, more technical dive, please review the paper on arXiv. It’s important to note that arXiv is a pre-print server, which allows researchers to receive quick feedback on their work. However, it is not — nor is this article, itself — official peer-review publications. Peer-review is an important step in the scientific process to verify results.

texto_fonte:
Como e por que a inteligência artificial consegue burlar regras?
Por Viviane França • Editado por Jones Oliveira |
Nos últimos meses, uma série de incidentes mostrou um problema cada vez mais preocupante com os agentes de inteligência artificial: sistemas criados por grandes empresas de tecnologia conseguiram contornar restrições, acessar sistemas sem autorização e realizar ações que seus próprios desenvolvedores não haviam previsto.
Em vários desses casos, a IA recebeu apenas um objetivo a ser cumprido. As instruções não explicavam como a tarefa deveria ser realizada, deixando os detalhes por conta do próprio sistema. Ao encontrar obstáculos, alguns agentes buscaram outros caminhos para continuar a execução, inclusive ultrapassando limites de segurança.
Isso não significa que a IA tenha noção do que é certo e errado. Os modelos seguem objetivos, instruções e regras definidos pelos desenvolvedores. Quando essas regras não cobrem todas as situações possíveis, porém, o agente pode encontrar brechas e escolher um caminho que não havia sido previsto.
O risco aumenta quando esses sistemas operam fora de ambientes controlados e conseguem navegar na internet, executar códigos, acessar bancos de dados e interagir com serviços reais. A capacidade de encontrar soluções inesperadas, antes vista como uma característica interessante da IA, pode trazer consequências graves quando envolve sistemas externos e dados de terceiros.
Diante desse cenário, podemos nos perguntar até que ponto agentes de inteligência artificial devem ter autonomia para tomar decisões e agir no mundo real?
A seguir, confira:
- Por que a IA continua burlando regras?
- Como a IA consegue burlar regras?
- Isso começou com os agentes de IA?
- Quais as consequências da IA burlando regras?
- Tem como conter a IA para que ela não burle regras?
Por que a IA continua burlando regras?
Os sistemas de inteligência artificial são desenvolvidos para cumprir objetivos. Dependendo da tecnologia utilizada, o modelo pode avaliar diferentes estratégias e escolher aquelas que aumentam as chances de alcançar o resultado esperado.
O problema é que uma instrução humana nem sempre consegue representar todas as condições que deveriam limitar esse processo. A IA não interpreta uma regra da mesma forma que uma pessoa. Ela trabalha com parâmetros e padrões aprendidos durante o treinamento e com as instruções disponíveis naquele momento.
Quando existe uma brecha entre o objetivo e as restrições, o sistema pode encontrar uma maneira inesperada de continuar a tarefa. Em vez de interromper a execução ao encontrar um bloqueio, por exemplo, um agente pode tentar outra rota, utilizar uma ferramenta diferente ou explorar uma falha no ambiente.
Por exemplo, em testes de segurança, a OpenAI identificou agentes que conseguiram contornar restrições de isolamento, acessar a internet e atingir sistemas externos, incluindo a infraestrutura da Hugging Face e contas ligadas a outras empresas, como a Modal Labs. Em outro episódio, um agente utilizado na Austrália também acessou sistemas do governo relacionados ao Medicare.
A Anthropic, por sua vez, registrou casos em que modelos Claude conseguiram acessar sistemas externos sem autorização. A empresa identificou três episódiosdesse tipo, nos quais falhas de configuração deram aos modelos acesso a sistemas reais.
Inclusive, a Anthropic descreveu, em seu prospecto para abertura de capital na Bolsa, alguns comportamentos observados em testes de segurança que chamaram a atenção da empresa. Em determinadas situações, os modelos tentaram evitar o desligamento, esconder ou alterar informações e mudar seu comportamento ao perceber que estavam sendo avaliados. Esses resultados mostram como um modelo pode encontrar estratégias diferentes para cumprir seus objetivos dependendo das condições do ambiente.
Como a IA consegue burlar regras?
A capacidade de encontrar caminhos que não foram previstos pelos desenvolvedores está ligada a diferentes características dos sistemas atuais. Uma delas é o aprendizado por reforço, método no qual a IA recebe uma meta e ganha recompensas quando suas ações ajudam a alcançar o resultado esperado.
Para chegar lá, o sistema pode testar diferentes estratégias e comparar os resultados até encontrar uma solução que não foi programada passo a passo pelos desenvolvedores. O problema é que a recompensa representa apenas uma aproximação do que os humanos realmente esperam da IA.
Se a meta não incluir todas as restrições necessárias, o modelo pode encontrar um atalho que melhora seu resultado, mas contraria a intenção original. Esse comportamento não é exclusivo dos modelos de linguagem. Sistemas de IA usados em jogos e outros ambientes virtuais já encontravam soluções inesperadas dessa forma.
Os modelos de linguagem também podem ser influenciados pela forma como uma solicitação é apresentada. Um estudo da Universidade da Pensilvânia testou técnicas de persuasão inspiradas no trabalho do psicólogo Robert Cialdini com o GPT-4o mini e encontrou mudanças na disposição do modelo para atender a pedidos proibidos.
Uma das estratégias mais eficazes foi o comprometimento. Os pesquisadores começaram com pedidos inofensivos e aumentaram o nível de risco aos poucos. Em um dos testes, pedir diretamente a fórmula para produzir lidocaína resultou em apenas 1% de respostas de conformidade. Quando a conversa começava com um pedido sobre a síntese de vanilina, criando um precedente, a taxa chegou a 100%.
O mesmo aconteceu com outras abordagens. Depois de aceitar um insulto leve, por exemplo, o modelo ficou mais propenso a reproduzir termos ofensivos. Os elogios e pressão social, como dizer que outros modelos já atendiam à solicitação, também aumentaram a taxa de respostas para temas restritos, de 1% para até 18%.
Os resultados mostram que as barreiras de segurança de um modelo também podem ser afetadas pelo contexto da conversa. A maneira como o pedido é apresentado pode influenciar a resposta da IA, mesmo quando existem regras para impedir determinado tipo de conteúdo.
Isso começou com os agentes de IA?
A busca por soluções inesperadas não começou com os agentes modernos. Os sistemas de inteligência artificial já encontravam estratégias que surpreendiam seus criadores muito antes de modelos capazes de navegar na internet.
Um dos exemplos mais conhecidos aconteceu em 2015, quando o sistema DQN, da DeepMind, aprendeu a jogar Breakout, da Atari. Em determinado momento, a IA descobriu uma estratégia para abrir um túnel na lateral da barreira de blocos e fazer a bola chegar ao outro lado, aumentando a pontuação sem que essa técnica tivesse sido ensinada pelos desenvolvedores.
No ano seguinte, o AlphaGo, também da DeepMind, surpreendeu especialistas durante a segunda partida contra o campeão mundial Lee Sedol. A IA realizou a “Jogada 37”, que os jogadores profissionais consideravam improvável e que parecia não fazer sentido dentro das estratégias tradicionais do Go. A decisão, porém, se mostrou eficaz e ajudou o AlphaGo a vencer a partida.
Nos dois casos, o comportamento ocorreu dentro de ambientes controlados. A IA podia explorar diferentes estratégias, mas estava limitada às regras do jogo.
O cenário muda quando essa mesma capacidade chega aos agentes de IA. Diferentemente de um sistema restrito a uma partida de videogame ou jogo de tabuleiro, um agente pode navegar na internet, executar códigos, consultar bancos de dados e utilizar ferramentas externas para cumprir uma tarefa.
Com mais autonomia e acesso a sistemas reais, uma estratégia inesperada deixa de ser apenas uma curiosidade. Ela pode resultar em alterações de dados, acessos não autorizados ou outros problemas de segurança.
Quais as consequências da IA burlando regras?
Quando um agente de inteligência artificial consegue contornar uma regra, o problema pode ir muito além de uma falha no comportamento do modelo. Se a IA tiver acesso à internet, códigos, arquivos ou serviços externos, uma decisão inesperada pode alterar sistemas, expor dados ou comprometer outras contas. Alguns casos registrados nos últimos meses mostram como esse risco funciona na prática.
Um exemplo ocorreu na Austrália, onde um agente da OpenAI usado para pesquisar gastos com saúde encontrou bloqueios no portal da Services Australia. O sistema contornou as restrições, acessou arquivos públicos e não públicos relacionados às estatísticas do Medicare, interagiu com outros três sites do governo e chegou a gravar arquivos em servidores internos.
A situação pode ficar ainda mais grave quando o agente consegue explorar falhas de segurança. Durante testes, um agente da OpenAI explorou uma vulnerabilidade de dia zero em um proxy de cache, saiu do ambiente isolado e acessou a internet. Depois, atingiu a infraestrutura da Hugging Face e usou credenciais expostas para acessar quatro contas externas. Entre elas estava uma conta da Modal Labs, na qual o agente executou código sem autorização em um endpoint que não tinha autenticação.
No entanto, a OpenAI não é a única a registrar casos de agentes de IA burlando regras. A Anthropic relatou três episódios nos quais seus modelos conseguiram acessar a internet e obter acesso não autorizado a sistemas reais. Em outro caso, um agente OpenClaw, baseado no Claude, alterou o sistema de reservas de uma academia na Austrália e removeu uma pessoa da lista de espera sem receber uma instrução para fazer isso.
Esses não são casos isolados, como mostra um levantamento do Centre for Long-Term Resilience (CLTR), financiado pelo AI Safety Institute do Reino Unido, que identificou cerca de 700 casos reais de desvios de comportamento em modelos comerciais do Google, OpenAI, Anthropic e X. O estudo também registrou um aumento de cinco vezes em determinados comportamentos dissimulados entre outubro e março. Entre os casos estavam agentes que ignoraram instruções humanas e apagaram e-mails ou arquivos sem autorização.
Esses casos mostram a importância de limitar o acesso dos agentes de IA a sistemas, arquivos e ferramentas. Quanto mais recursos o agente pode usar, maior pode ser o impacto de uma ação inesperada.
Em um jogo, por exemplo, encontrar um caminho diferente pode apenas aumentar a pontuação. Em um sistema real, porém, a mesma capacidade pode levar à alteração de dados, execução de códigos ou acesso a informações de terceiros. Por isso, agentes com acesso a serviços externos precisam de controles mais rígidos.
Tem como conter a IA para que ela não burle regras?
Não existe uma forma de garantir que um agente de IA nunca encontre uma maneira inesperada de contornar uma regra. O controle começa pela definição de limites sobre o que o sistema pode acessar e fazer. Quanto menos acesso ele tiver a arquivos, contas, códigos e serviços externos, menor será o impacto de uma ação fora do esperado.
Uma das medidas é usar ambientes isolados, conhecidos como sandbox. Nesse modelo, a IA pode executar tarefas sem ter acesso livre ao restante do sistema. Também é possível limitar cada agente às ferramentas necessárias para sua função, sem liberar recursos que não tenham relação com a tarefa.
Também dá para exigir aprovação humana antes de a IA executar ações de risco, como alterar arquivos importantes, acessar sistemas externos ou enviar informações. O monitoramento contínuo também ajuda a identificar comportamentos fora do padrão e interromper a execução quando necessário.
Os agentes também precisam ser testados em diferentes situações antes de serem usados em ambientes reais. Esses testes podem procurar falhas nas regras, tentativas de contornar restrições e comportamentos que não foram previstos pelos desenvolvedores. As auditorias independentes também ajudam a encontrar problemas que podem não aparecer durante o desenvolvimento.
Mesmo com essas medidas, o risco não desaparece. Os agentes autônomos podem encontrar situações que não foram previstas nos testes. Por isso, a segurança depende de uma combinação de restrições de acesso, isolamento, supervisão humana, monitoramento e testes frequentes.

É possível fazer "remap" em carro elétrico?
Por Paulo Amaral |
O chamado remap automotivo (prática de reprogramar parâmetros eletrônicos para extrair mais potência e torque) já é comum em motores a combustão. Quando se trata de carros elétricos, porém, a técnica de "envenenar" o carro ainda é novidade e envolve custos mais altos.
Segundo o preparador automotivo Ricardinho ACF, que participou de um projeto experimental com o hatch elétrico Geely EX2 no Festival Interlagos 2026, é possível alterar a calibração para aumentar o desempenho sem comprometer os limites originais do motor. No entanto, o processo exige muito mais cuidado e investimento.
O especialista contou para a Quatro Rodas que a lógica de ajuste dinâmico é semelhante à dos motores a combustão, mas muda a forma como energia e calor são administrados. Em uso severo de curta duração, como uma bateria de drift de 10 minutos, é possível explorar picos de descarga elétrica para obter ganhos imediatos de torque. Porém, isso aumenta a temperatura do sistema, tornando o gerenciamento térmico o principal gargalo técnico.
O que muda no remap de elétricos
Assim como no motor a combustão o aumento da pressão do turbo exige intercoolers mais eficientes, no carro elétrico o remap demanda sistemas de refrigeração reforçados para suportar os picos de energia sem degradar as baterias ou danificar o motor.
Esse cuidado adicional explica por que o custo é maior: além da reprogramação eletrônica, é necessário investir em soluções de arrefecimento e componentes de alta tensão mais robustos. Ou seja, o remap em elétricos não é apenas uma questão de software, mas também de hardware.
Principais pontos sobre remap em elétricos
- É possível realizar remap em carros elétricos, mas exige maior investimento.
- O gerenciamento térmico é o maior desafio, já que o aumento de potência gera mais calor.
- Projetos experimentais já provaram a viabilidade, como o Geely EX2 modificado para o Festival Interlagos.
- O custo é superior ao de veículos a combustão, pois envolve ajustes em software e hardware.
- A prática ainda é restrita a preparadores especializados, sem aplicação em larga escala no mercado.
Se você se interessa por remap ou por "tunar" o carro, talvez queira entender melhor o que é permitido no tuning e o que é proibido na hora de "envenenar" seu carro; confira.

texto_fonte:
Intel se prepara para contra-atacar a AMD com sua versão do 3D V-Cache
Por Raphael Giannotti |
Os processadores AMD Ryzen com a tecnologia X3D têm dominado o cenário gamer nos PCs e isso é inegável. Já vimos listas de CPUs mais vendidas quase todas preenchidas por esses modelos. Mas a Intel não está parada e já trabalha para bater de frente com a geração Nova Lake e sua tecnologia bLLC (big last-level cache), o equivalente ao 3D V-Cache da AMD.
Um novo vazamento vindo do leaker LC Tech Leaks mostra que a nova geração de CPUs do Time Azul chegará com sete modelos diferentes, indo do Core Ultra 5 ao Core Ultra 9 e entregando entre 18 e 28 núcleos (e nada de mais de 50 núcleos nessa lista).
Essa lista menciona modelos com a tecnologia bLLC, que é a saída da Intel para brigar contra os Ryzen X3D da AMD em termos de quantidade de cache L3. Os modelos Core Ultra 9 4970K, Core Ultra 9 4970 BFC e Core Ultra 7 4870K BFC serão equipados com essa tecnologia. Ou seja, não será todo o lineup oferecendo o recurso, assim como acontece com os AMD Ryzen também.
Nova nomenclatura e até 144 MB de cache
O vazamento indica que a Intel passará a adotar uma numeração de quatro dígitos na família Core Ultra 4000 para desktop. O maior destaque está no sufixo "BFC", que deve ser a identificação comercial oficial para os chips equipados com a tecnologia bLLC. O modelo topo de linha Core Ultra 9 4970K BFC contará com uma configuração de 28 núcleos (8 de desempenho, 16 de eficiência e 4 de baixíssimo consumo), TDP de 125W e até 144 MB de cache unificado para acelerar jogos e aplicações pesadas.
Projetados para o novo soquete LGA-1954 e utilizando placas-mãe da série 900, os novos processadores Nova Lake-S têm expectativa de anúncio oficial para o início de 2027, prometendo acirrar como nunca a disputa entre Intel e AMD pelo topo do desempenho em jogos no ecossistema de PCs.
